First Chapter: The First Discourse on Kassapa [The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Kassapa, when a bhikkhu is possessed of five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (3) He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and provisions for the sick. (4) He is energetic in abandoning unwholesome states and arousing wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. (5) He is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. When a bhikkhu is possessed of these five qualities, he is capable of achieving the destruction of the taints in this very life. [The Venerable Mahākassapa then asked: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not? “Kassapa, it is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to serenity that lead to dwelling in comfort. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, seclusion of the body. (2) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, concentration of the mind. (3) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the various kinds of supernormal power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as if through space; he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without sinking as if it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels in space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; he exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahma world. (4) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human. He hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near. (5) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the knowledge of the minds of other beings, of other persons. He understands a mind affected by lust as affected by lust, and a mind unaffected by lust as unaffected by lust; he understands a mind affected by hate as affected by hate, and a mind unaffected by hate as unaffected by hate; he understands a mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion, and a mind unaffected by delusion as unaffected by delusion; he understands a contracted mind as contracted, and a distracted mind as distracted; he understands an exalted mind as exalted, and an unexalted mind as unexalted; he understands a surpassed mind as surpassed, and an unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed; he understands a concentrated mind as concentrated, and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; he understands a liberated mind as liberated, and an unliberated mind as unliberated. It is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to serenity that lead to dwelling in comfort, that some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not. [The Venerable Mahākassapa then asked: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not? “Kassapa, it is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to insight that lead to dwelling in comfort. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the appearance of a vision of forms internally. (2) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the appearance of a vision of forms externally. (3) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the appearance of a vision of forms internally and externally. (4) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the appearance of a vision of forms that are beautiful and ugly. (5) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the appearance of a vision of forms that are varied and immeasurable.

It is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to insight that lead to dwelling in comfort, that some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not. [The Venerable Mahākassapa then asked: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not? “Kassapa, it is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to the higher mind that lead to dwelling in comfort. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the base of infinite space. (2) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the base of infinite consciousness. (3) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the base of nothingness. (4) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. (5) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the cessation of perception and feeling. It is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to the higher mind that lead to dwelling in comfort, that some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not. [The Venerable Mahākassapa then asked: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not? “Kassapa, it is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to the higher wisdom that lead to dwelling in comfort. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the recollection of past lives, their aspects and particulars. (2) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human. (3) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings. (4) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. (5) Having known the destruction of the taints, he gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless through the destruction of the taints. It is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to the higher wisdom that lead to dwelling in comfort, that some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not. [The Venerable Mahākassapa then asked: “But, Bhante, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some bhikkhus here achieve the destruction of the taints in this very life, while others do not? “Kassapa, it is because they do not gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, these five factors conducive to the higher knowledge that lead to dwelling in comfort. What five? (1) Here, Kassapa, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the first jhāna, which is secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, and accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. (2) With the subsiding of thought and examination, he gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, when the night had advanced, the young deity Kassapa, of surpassing beauty, illuminated the entirety of Jeta’s Grove.
Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Kassapa said this to the Blessed One:
"The Blessed One has explained what a bhikkhu is, but he has not given instruction on how to become a bhikkhu."
“In that case, Kassapa, let what occurs to you on this matter be spoken.
“One should train in well-spoken words and in attending upon ascetics.”
"And solitude for one who sits alone,
and the calming of the mind"—
this is what the deva-son Kassapa said.
The Teacher gave his approval.
Then the young deva Kassapa, thinking, "The Teacher has approved of me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.2 (SN 2.2, SN 83, PTS [1st ed. SN i 46; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 105)*
1. First Chapter:
The Second Kassapa Discourse.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, the young deva Kassapa recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“If a bhikkhu should be a meditator with a liberated mind,
he might wish for the attainment of his heart’s desire.”
“Having understood the world’s arising and passing away, one of pure mind is then independent of its rewards.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.3 (SN 2.3, SN 84, PTS [1st ed. SN i 47; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 105)
1. First Chapter:
The Discourse on Māgha.
Setting at Sāvatthī.

Then, when the night had advanced, the young deity Māgha, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deity Māgha addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“What must one cut off to sleep in happiness?”
“What is it that, when cut off,
one does not grieve? Of what single thing,
O Gotama, do you approve the destruction?”
“Having cut off anger, one sleeps happily;
having cut off anger, one does not grieve.
Of anger, which has poison as its root—”
The noble ones praise the slaying of one whose tip is sweet;
for having cut that off, one does not grieve.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.4 (SN 2.4, SN 85, PTS [1st ed. SN i 47, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 106) 1.
First Chapter: The Magadhan Discourse (Māgadhasutta)
At Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, the Māgadhaka deva-son addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“How many lamps are there in the world?”
By these things the world is illumined;
having approached you, O Blessed One,
to ask about this, how shall we understand it?
“There are four lamps in the world;
a fifth is not found here: the sun shines by day, [the moon shines by night, fire shines by both day and night, and the Dhamma shines by both day and night].”
The moon shines by night;
but the fire illuminates both day and night, shining here and there.
“The Perfectly Awakened One is the best of those who shine;
this is the unsurpassed radiance.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.5 (SN 2.5, SN 86, PTS [1st ed. SN i 47, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 107)*
1. First Chapter:
The Discourse to Dāmali.
Setting at Sāvatthī.

Then, when the night had advanced, the young deva Dāmali, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Dāmali recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“This is what ought to be done by a brahmin...”
One should exert oneself without weariness;
by the complete relinquishing of sensual desires,
one does not long for existence through that.
“There is nothing more to be done for the brahmin,” said the Blessed One,
“for the brahmin has accomplished what was to be done.”
As long as a person has not found a firm footing in the rivers,
they struggle with all their limbs;
but having found a footing, he stands secure on dry land.
For he has gone to the further shore and does not pull back.
This is the simile for the brahmin who has destroyed the taints, who is prudent and meditative.
Having reached the end of birth and death,
he does not strive further,
for he has gone to the further shore. (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.6)
1. First Chapter: The Discourse on the Giver of Desires.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, the young deity Kāmada said this to the Blessed One:
“It is difficult, Blessed One; it is very difficult, Blessed One. “They do indeed perform what is difficult,” [said the Blessed One].
"Those in training who are concentrated in virtue, O Blessed One,
through their steadfastness have entered the homeless life."
“Contentment brings happiness.
“It is rare, Blessed One, to find such contentment.
“They do indeed obtain what is rare.”
"Those who delight in the calming of the mind, both by day and by night," said the Blessed One, "are free from craving."
“The mind delights in meditation.
“This mind, Blessed One, is difficult to concentrate.
“Even though it is difficult to concentrate, they do concentrate it.”
"Those who delight in the tranquility of the faculties, O Blessed One,
having cut through the net of Death,"
“The Noble Ones go along giving [the gift of] desire.
“It is difficult to traverse, Blessed One; it is an uneven path.
“Whether it be difficult to traverse or uneven, [the Noble Ones go].”
The noble ones go where they wish;
the ignoble fall headlong upon the uneven path.
The path is equal for the noble ones;
for the noble ones are even amidst the uneven.
1. First Chapter:
The Discourse on Pañcālacaṇḍa.
Setting at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, the young deva Pañcālacaṇḍa recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Truly, in a crowded place,
the one of vast wisdom, Avindi, has found space;”
“The Buddha who awakened to jhāna,
the Sage, the Bull-like One who has withdrawn.
“Even in a crowded place they find [peace],” he said.
(The Blessed One [said]:
“The Dhamma for the attainment of Nibbāna,
O Pañcālacaṇḍā, for those who have attained mindfulness.”
“You are rightly well-composed,” [said the Blessed One].
*Saṁyutta Nikāya* 2.8 (SN 2.8, SN 89, PTS [1st ed. SN i 49, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 111) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
The Tāyana Sutta.
The setting was Sāvatthī.
Then the young deva Tāyana, formerly a founder of a religious sect, at the end of the night, having attained a most excellent beauty, [illuminated] the entire extent of...
Having illuminated Jeta’s Grove, he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Tāyana recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Exerting yourself, cut the stream;”
O Brahmin, cast away sensual desires;
for a sage who has not abandoned sensual desires does not attain singleness.
If one should do it, let one do it;
exert oneself firmly in this.
For a wandering life lived in laxity—
Only stirs up more dust.
An evil deed left undone is better,
for an evil deed brings remorse later on.
Better is a deed well done,
for having done which one does not regret;
like kusa grass when wrongly grasped.
He cuts his very own hand;
the ascetic life, when wrongly grasped,
drags one toward hell.
Whatever action is lax,
whatever vow is defiled,
and a holy life that is dubious—
“That does not bear great fruit.
This is what the young deva Tāyana said.
Having spoken thus, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

"Bhikkhus, during this night, a son of the gods named Tāyana, formerly a founder of other sects, at the end of the night, having illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove with his surpassing beauty, approached me; having approached,..."
Having paid homage to me, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, monks, the young deva Tāyana recited these verses in my presence:
“Exerting yourself, cut the stream;”
O Brahmin, cast away sensual desires;
for the sage who has not abandoned sensual desires does not attain singleness of being.
If one would do it, let one do it;
exert oneself firmly in this.
For a wandering life lived in laxity—
Only further stirs up the dust.
It is better that an evil deed be left undone;
for an evil deed brings torment later on.
Better is a deed well done,
which one does not regret after having done it;
like kusa grass when wrongly grasped, [it cuts the hand].
He cuts his very own hand;
the ascetic life, when wrongly grasped,
drags one down to hell.
Whatever action is slack,
whatever vow is defiled,
and whatever holy life is dubious—
"That does not bear great fruit.
This, monks, is what the young deva Tāyana said. Having spoken this, he paid homage to me, kept me on his right, and vanished right there.
Monks, you should learn the verses of Tāyana.
“Bhikkhus, master these Tāyanagāthā verses; memorize them, bhikkhus.
These Tāyanagāthā verses are beneficial and pertain to the fundamentals of the holy life.”
Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.9 (SN 2.9, SN 90, PTS [1st ed. SN i 50, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 114) 1.
First Chapter: The Moon Discourse (Candimasutta)
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now on that occasion the young deva Candima had been seized by Rāhu, the lord of the asuras.
Then the young deva Candima, recollecting the Blessed One, on that occasion uttered this verse:
"Homage to you, O Buddha, O Hero!
You are utterly liberated in every respect;
I am one who has entered upon a narrow path."
“May he be my refuge.
Then the Blessed One, concerning the young deity Candima, addressed Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, with this verse:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat...”
Candima has gone for refuge;
O Rāhu, release the moon!
The Buddhas are compassionate toward the world.

Then Rāhu, lord of the asuras, having released the divine son Canda, approached Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, in great haste. Having approached, agitated and with his hair standing on end, he stood to one side.
As he stood there, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, addressed him in verse:
"Why are you hurrying so?"
“Rāhu, you release the moon;
having come here with a look of agitation,
why do you stand as if afraid?”
“My head would split into seven pieces,
and while living I would find no happiness,
were I not sung of in the verses of the Buddha.”
"If he does not release his splendor.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.10 (SN 2.10, SN 91, PTS [1st ed. SN i 51; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 115) 1.
First Chapter (Paṭhamavagga)
The Sūriya Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, the young deva Sūriya had been seized by Rāhu, the lord of the asuras.
Then the divine son Sūriya, recollecting the Blessed One, on that occasion spoke this verse:
"Homage to you, O Buddha, O Hero!
You are utterly liberated in every respect."
“I am proceeding toward a narrow path;
may you be my refuge.
Then the Blessed One addressed Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, with verses concerning Sūriya, the son of the gods:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat,
the Sun— Rāhu has gone to him for refuge;
release the Sun, Rāhu!”
The Buddhas are compassionate toward the world.
He who is the maker of light in the darkness and gloom,
Vairocana, the radiant one of blazing splendor;
"Do not swallow the sun while moving through the sky, Rāhu!
Release my offspring, Rāhu, the sun!

Then Rāhu, lord of the asuras, released the divine son Sūriya and, in great haste, approached Vepacitti, lord of the asuras. Having approached him, agitated and with his hair standing on end, he stood to one side.
As Rāhu, lord of the asuras, was standing to one side, Vepacitti, lord of the asuras, addressed him in verse:
“Why indeed, Rāhu, do you release the sun in such a hurry?”
“Having come here looking so agitated,
why do you stand as if terrified?
“My head would split into seven pieces.”
Living, I find no happiness;
I have been sung to by the verses of the Buddha,
and I shall not escape the sun."
The First Chapter.
Its summary:
The two Kassapas and Māgha.
Māgadha, Dāmali, Kāmada,
Pañcālacaṇḍa, and Tāyana—
these ten are [the disciples] of Candima and Sūriya.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.11 (SN 2.11, SN 92, PTS [1st ed. SN i 51, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 117) 2. Anāthapiṇḍika-vagga Candimasa Sutta: To Candimasa At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Candimasa approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Householder, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he is one who has arrived at the fruit, one who has reached the goal, one for whom the task is done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one whose tethers to existence are completely severed, one who is liberated through final knowledge. What four? “Here, householder, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. “When a noble disciple possesses these four things, householder, he is one who has arrived at the fruit, one who has reached the goal, one for whom the task is done, one who has laid down the burden, one who has attained his own goal, one whose tethers to existence are completely severed, one who is liberated through final knowledge. When this was said, the householder Candimasa said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Blessed One has expounded the Dhamma in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the higher ordination! Then the householder Candimasa received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the higher ordination. And soon, not long after his higher ordination, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Candimasa, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Candimasa became one of the arahants.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then, when the night had advanced, the young deity Candimasa, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Candimasa recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“They indeed will go in safety,
like deer in a secure marsh.”
“Having attained the jhānas,
unified, prudent, and mindful—
these indeed shall go to the further shore.”
Like a lotus that has burst through its web,
having attained the meditative absorptions,
those who are heedful abandon all conflict.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.12 (SN 2.12, SN 93, PTS [1st ed. SN i 52, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 118) 2. Anāthapiṇḍika-vagga Veṇḍu Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the householder Veṇḍu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Householder, if you were asked: ‘How many kinds of persons are there in the world? how would you answer? “Bhante, if I were asked that, I would answer: ‘There are four kinds of persons in the world. “But which four? “There is the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “Good, householder! Good, householder! There are indeed these four kinds of persons in the world. (1) “And what, householder, is the person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, someone develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving, but he does not teach the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it. This is called the person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. (2) “And what is the person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, someone develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to energy and volitional formations of striving, but he does not teach the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it. This is called the person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. (3) “And what is the person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, someone develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to mind and volitional formations of striving, but he does not teach the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it. This is called the person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. (4) “And what is the person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, someone develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving, and he teaches the Dhamma to others in detail as he has heard it and learned it. This is called the person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. These, householder, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the householder Veṇḍu said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! ... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
Standing to one side, the young deva Veṇḍu recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Happy indeed are those people who attend upon the Sugata.”
"Applying myself to the teaching of Gotama,
may I train with heedfulness.
"Those words of instruction spoken by me,"
(Thus said the Blessed One:
"The meditators train accordingly;
being diligent at the proper time,"
“They would not be subject to death.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.13 (SN 2.13, SN 94, PTS [1st ed. SN i 52, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 119) 2. Anāthapiṇḍika-vagga
The Long-Staff Discourse.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then, when the night had advanced, the young god Dīghalaṭṭhi, of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Veḷuvana, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young god Dīghalaṭṭhi recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“A bhikkhu might be a meditator with a liberated mind,
if he desires the attainment of the heart’s goal;
having understood the arising and passing away of the world,”
“With a well-disposed mind, one is not dependent;
this is the benefit then. — *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.14 (SN 2.14, SN 95, PTS [1st ed. SN i 52, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 120) 2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika
The Nandana Sutta.
Standing to one side, the young deva Nandana addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom:”
The Blessed One’s knowledge and vision is unobstructed.
Of what kind do they say one is virtuous?
Of what kind do they say one possesses wisdom?
“In what manner does one live having transcended suffering?
In what manner do the deities worship him?
“He who is virtuous, wise, and developed in self...”
Concentrated, delighting in meditation, and mindful;
all his sorrows have vanished and are abandoned—
he is one whose taints are destroyed, bearing his final body.
Such a person they call virtuous;
such a person they call wise;
such a person, having transcended suffering, dwells in peace.
“Such a one the deities worship.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.15 (SN 2.15, SN 96, PTS [1st ed. SN i 53, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 121) 2. Anāthapiṇḍika-vagga (The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika)
The Candana Sutta.
Standing to one side, the young deva Candana addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“How indeed does one cross the flood?”
“Who, being untiring day and night,
would not sink in the deep, which has no foothold and no support?”
“Always endowed with virtue,
wise and well-concentrated,
with energy aroused and resolute, [he is one who has crossed over the flood].”
He crosses the flood so difficult to cross,
being detached from the perception of sensual pleasure and having transcended the fetter of form.
"With delight and lust utterly destroyed, he does not sink in the deep.
— Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.16 (SN 2.16, SN 97, PTS [1st ed. SN i 53; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 122)
2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika.
The Vāsudattasutta.
Standing to one side, the young deva Vāsudatta recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
As if struck by a sword,
as if my head were on fire,
I strive for the abandonment of sensual lust.
“A mindful bhikkhu should wander forth.
Like one struck by a sword,
like one with fire burning on his head;
“For the abandoning of the view of a personal body, let a bhikkhu wander mindfully.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.17* (SN 2.17, SN 98, PTS [1st ed. SN i 53; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 122)
2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika:
The Subrahma Sutta.
Standing to one side, the young deva Subrahma addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“This mind is constantly terrified;
this intellect is constantly agitated,
even before difficulties have arisen.”
"And likewise when they have arisen—
if there is anything that is not afraid,
tell me that when I ask you."
“Nothing other than enlightenment, nothing other than austerity,
nothing other than restraint of the faculties,
and nothing other than the relinquishing of everything— ”
“I see the welfare of living beings.
This he said...
[and] right there he vanished.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.18 (SN 2.18, SN 99, PTS [1st ed. SN i 54, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 123) 2. Anāthapiṇḍikavagga Kakudhasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Kakudha approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell; while others, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? “Brahmin, it is because of volition, because of what has been willed, that beings come to be distinguished. “But, Master Gotama, what does one intend, what does one will, such that with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell? “Here, brahmin, having intended for one’s own affliction, one acts for the affliction of others; having intended for one’s own affliction, one acts for the affliction of both oneself and others. It is by having intended thus, by having willed thus, that with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the nether world, in hell. “But, Master Gotama, what does one intend, what does one will, such that with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? “Here, brahmin, having intended for one’s own welfare, one acts for one’s own welfare; having intended for one’s own welfare, one acts for the welfare of others; having intended for one’s own welfare, one acts for the welfare of both oneself and others. It is by having intended thus, by having willed thus, that with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. When this was said, the brahmin Kakudha said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... From today let Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others; the person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare; the person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others; and the person who is intent on his own welfare and also on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, someone develops concentration with the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human. With the divine ear element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near. This is how a person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, someone develops the mind of loving-kindness toward a certain direction, and so on, pervading the entire world, above, below, across, everywhere, all-around, with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. This is how a person is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, someone is immoral, of bad character, impure, of suspect behavior, secretive in his actions, not an ascetic though claiming to be one, not a celibate though claiming to be one, inwardly rotten, corrupt, depraved. This is how a person is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And how, bhikkhus, is a person intent on his own welfare and also on the welfare of others? Here, someone develops concentration with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is how a person is intent on his own welfare and also on the welfare of others. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus the Blessed One spoke. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had left, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus! “Friend! those bhikkhus replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, when the Blessed One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling after speaking this discourse, he had in mind these four kinds of persons. That is what the Venerable Ānanda said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Venerable Ānanda’s words. Thus have I heard. Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāketa in the Añjana Grove, the Deer Park.
Then the young deity Kakudha, at the end of the night, with a most excellent radiance, illuminated the entire Añjana Grove.
Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the deva-son Kakudha said this to the Blessed One:
“Are you joyful, ascetic?”
“What have you gained, friend?
“In that case, ascetic, you must grieve.
“What have you lost, friend?”
“In that case, ascetic, you neither rejoice nor do you grieve?
“It is so, friend.
“I hope you are free from affliction, monk?”
Is there no delight found?
Is dissatisfaction not overwhelming you as you sit all alone?”
“O Yakkha, I am indeed free from affliction,
and yet no delight is found in me;
even as I sit all alone— ”
“‘There is no displeasure, nor is there delight.
How is it, blameless monk, that there is no joy?
How does it not exist?”
“How is it that discontent does not overwhelm you as you sit alone?
“Indeed, for one born into misery, delight [arises]...”
For one who rejoices, there is indeed misfortune;
know this, friend: a bhikkhu who does not rejoice is free from misfortune.
“After a long time indeed,
I behold the brahmin who has attained final Nibbāna,
the monk who is joyless and free from blemish.”
"Having crossed over attachment to the three worlds.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.19 (SN 2.19, SN 100, PTS [1st ed. SN i 54, PTS [2nd ed.
SN i 125) 2. Anāthapiṇḍika Chapter
The Uttara Sutta;
its setting was Rājagaha.
Standing to one side, the young deva Uttara recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Life is being led away, its span is short;
for one led by old age, there are no refuges.
Seeing this danger in death,”
“One should perform meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
“Life is led away, its span is short;
for one led by old age, there is no refuge.”
“Perceiving this danger in death, one who seeks peace should abandon the bait of the world.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.20* (SN 2.20, SN 101, PTS [1st ed. SN i 55; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 126)
2. The Chapter on Anāthapiṇḍika:
The Discourse to Anāthapiṇḍika.
Standing to one side, the divine son Anāthapiṇḍika recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“This indeed is that Jeta’s Grove,
frequented by the assembly of seers;
it is inhabited by the King of Dhamma.”
It produces joy for me:
action, knowledge, and the Dhamma;
virtue is the supreme way of life.
By this mortals are purified,
not by lineage or wealth.
Therefore, a wise person...
Clearly perceiving one's own welfare,
one should investigate the Dhamma with systematic reflection;
in this way, one is purified therein.
Sāriputta indeed excels in wisdom,
in virtue, and in tranquility;
even that bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore, [is not his equal].
“...this much may be the limit.
This is what the young deva Anāthapiṇḍika said.
Having spoken thus, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, when that night had passed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, during this night, as the night was far advanced, a certain son of the gods of surpassing beauty, having illuminated the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached me;
having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side."
Standing to one side, monks, that son of the gods recited these verses in my presence:
“This indeed is that Jeta’s Grove,
frequented by the assembly of seers;”
It was inhabited by the King of Dhamma,
producing joy for me.
Action, clear knowledge, and Dhamma— these are the three.
Virtue is the supreme life;
by this mortals are purified,
not by lineage or wealth.
Therefore, indeed, a wise person,
seeing his own welfare,
should thoroughly investigate the Dhamma with systematic reflection.
Thus one is purified therein.
Sāriputta is supreme in wisdom,
as well as in virtue and tranquility.
"Even a bhikkhu who has gone to the further shore could be no more than this," said that son of the gods, monks. This is what he spoke.
“Having said this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One:
“Surely, Bhante, that must have been the deva-son Anāthapiṇḍika.”
“The householder Anāthapiṇḍika has gained deep confidence in the Venerable Sāriputta.
“Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You have attained as much as can be attained through reasoning, Ānanda.
For that one, Ānanda, is a son of the gods named Anāthapiṇḍika.”
The second chapter, the Anāthapiṇḍika Chapter.
Its summary verse: Candimasa, Veṇḍu, and...
Dīghalaṭṭhi and Nandana;
Candana and Vāsudatta,
Subrahmā and Kakudha.
Uttara was called the ninth;
the tenth was Anāthapiṇḍika.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.21 (SN 2.21, SN 102, PTS [1st ed. SN i 56, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 129).
3. Nānātitthiyavagga Sivasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the young deva Siva, in the late night, with a magnificent radiance that illuminated the entirety of Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Siva recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“One should associate only with the virtuous,
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the good, [one should dwell with them].”
One becomes better, not worse.
One should associate only with the virtuous;
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous.
Having understood the true Dhamma of the virtuous,
wisdom is obtained, and not from anyone else;
one should associate only with the wise.
One should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dharma of the good,
one does not grieve in the midst of sorrow.
One should associate only with the virtuous,
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the good.
One shines in the midst of kinsmen.
One should associate only with the virtuous;
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous.
Having understood the true Dhamma of the virtuous,
beings go to a happy destination;
one should associate only with the wise.
One should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dharma of the good,
beings abide in happiness.
Then the Blessed One replied to the young deva Siva with a verse:
“One should associate only with the virtuous;
one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous.”
“Having understood the true Dhamma, one is liberated from all suffering.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.22 (SN 2.22, SN 103; PTS [1st ed. SN i 57; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 131)
3. Nānātitthiyavagga Khemasutta Standing to one side,
the young deity Khema recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Fools of little intelligence wander about with themselves as their own enemies,
performing evil deeds.”
Whatever action has a bitter fruit—
that deed is not well done,
for having done it, one regrets it.
Whose face, weeping with tears,
experiences the result—
that action was well done.
That which, having done, one does not regret,
and whose ripening one experiences with a joyful and glad mind.
One should do beforehand that which one knows to be for one's own welfare;
not with the deliberation of a cartwright.
The wise person should persevere with mindfulness,
just as a cartwright, having abandoned a worn-out, uneven path, follows the great highway.
Having ascended a rugged path,
he meditates like one whose axle is broken;
even so, having departed from the Dhamma...
Following after what is unrighteous,
the dull-witted one has entered the jaws of death and sits brooding like one whose axle is broken.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.23 (SN 2.23, SN 104, PTS [1st ed. SN i 57, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 132) 3. Nānātitthiyavagga Serīsutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the wanderer Serisaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Serisaka said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell? And what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world? “Serisaka, it is because of three things that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. What three? Here, Serisaka, someone destroys life, takes what is not given, and engages in sexual misconduct. It is because of these three things that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of misery, in a bad destination, in the lower world, in hell. It is because of three other things, Serisaka, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. What three? Here, Serisaka, someone abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, and abstains from sexual misconduct. It is because of these three things that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. When this was said, the wanderer Serisaka said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... From today let Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
Standing to one side, the young deva Serī addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Both gods and humans alike delight only in food;”
“Then who indeed is that yakkha whom he does not delight in?
“Those who give it with faith,” [he replied].
With a serene mind,
one partakes of that very food both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, having overcome stinginess,
one who has conquered impurity should give gifts;
for merits follow one in the world beyond.
“They are the support for living beings.
“It is wonderful, Bhante; it is marvelous, Bhante!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One:”
“Whatever food they give with faith,
with a mind full of serene confidence,
that very food attends upon him.”
In this world and in the next.
Therefore, having overcome stinginess,
one who has conquered impurity should give gifts.
“Meritorious deeds are the foundation for living beings in the world beyond.
“Venerable sir, in the past I was a king named Sirī, a giver, a master of generosity, one who spoke in praise of giving.”
“Venerable sir, alms were being given by me at my four gates to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars.
Then, venerable sir, the women of the harem approached me and said:
‘Alms are being given to the King, but no alms are being given to us.’”
"It would be well if we too, by depending on this deity, were to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
"I am indeed a giver, a master of giving, and one who speaks in praise of giving."
"If one says, 'I shall give a gift,' what would you say?
"In that case, venerable sir, I gave the first gate to the women's quarters.
There, a gift was given to the women's quarters, and my gift was turned back."
Then, Bhante, the subordinate khattiyas approached me and said this:
“The King’s gift is being given; the harem’s gift is being given; but our gift is not being given.
It would be well, Your Majesty, if we too, depending on the King, might give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.”
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to me:
“I am indeed a donor, a master of giving, one who speaks in praise of giving.
When someone says, ‘I shall give a gift,’ what should I say?”
"So, venerable sir, I gave the second gate to the khattiya followers.
There, gifts were given to the khattiya followers, but my own gift was turned back.
Then, venerable sir, the army approached me and said this:"
‘Gifts are being given to the King; gifts are being given to the women’s quarters; gifts are being given to the subordinate kshatriyas; but no gifts are being given to us.
It would be well if we too, by relying on the King, were to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
‘I am indeed a donor, a master of giving, one who speaks in praise of generosity.
When someone says, “I shall give a gift,” what should I say?’—
it was with this thought, venerable sir, that I gave the third gate to the army.
There, alms were given to the army, but my gift was refused.
Then, venerable sir, the brahmins and householders approached me and said this:

“Alms are being given to Your Majesty; alms are being given to the women’s quarters; alms are being given to the khattiya followers; alms are being given to the army; but no alms are being given to us.”
"It would be well if we too, by relying on this deity, were to give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
Then, venerable sir, this occurred to me:
"I am indeed a donor, a master of giving, and one who speaks in praise of generosity."
"If someone were to say, 'I will give a gift,' what would you say?
"In that case, venerable sir, I would have given the fourth door to the brahmin householders.
There, gifts were given by the brahmin householders, but my gift was turned back."
Then, venerable sir, men approached me and said this:
“No gift is being given to the King now.
When they had spoken thus, venerable sir, I said this to those men:

"In that case, my man, whatever income is generated in the outlying provinces, let half be brought into the inner palace and let half be given right there as alms to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the needy, the destitute, and beggars. "Venerable sir,
I have not reached the limit of those merits performed over such a long time, nor of those wholesome states practiced over such a long time— I cannot determine how much merit there is,
or what the extent of the result of that merit is, or for how long I shall remain in heaven."
It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One:
“Those who give with faith...”
With a serene mind,
one partakes of that very food both in this world and in the next.
Therefore, having overcome stinginess and conquered defilement,
one should give gifts;
for merits follow one in the world beyond.
“They become a refuge for living beings.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.24 (SN 2.24, SN 105, PTS [1st ed. SN i 60, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 137) 3.
Nānātitthiyavagga (The Chapter on Various Sectarians)
The Discourse to Ghaṭīkāra.
Standing to one side, the young deity Ghaṭīkāra recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“We have been reborn in the Aviha heaven.”
The seven monks are liberated;
with lust and hatred utterly destroyed,
they have crossed over the attachment to the world.
“And who are those who have crossed the mire,
the realm of death so difficult to cross?
Who, having left behind the human body,”
"Upaka, Palagaṇḍa, and Pukkusāti— these three have transcended divine yoga."
Bhaddiya, Khaṇḍadeva, Bāhu, Aggigavesī,
and Saṅgīti— they, having abandoned the human body, [attained the state of non-returning].
“‘You have transcended divine yoga’—
you speak rightly of those who have abandoned Mara’s snares.”
“Having understood whose Dhamma did they sever the bond of existence?
“None other than the Blessed One.”
None other than your teaching;
having understood your Dhamma,
they have severed the bond of existence.
Having understood here that Dhamma wherein both name-and-form cease without remainder—
“He has severed the bond of existence.
“You speak words that are profound,
difficult to discern, and very hard to understand.”
“Having understood whose Dhamma do you speak such words?
“In the past, I was a potter;”
In Vekaḷiṅga, I was Ghaṭīkāra;
I was a supporter of my mother and father,
a lay follower of Kassapa.
Abstaining from sexual intercourse,
practicing the holy life, and free from worldly desires,
he was a native of your own town.
Formerly you were my friend.
Now I recognize these seven bhikkhus as liberated.
“When lust and hatred are utterly destroyed, one has crossed over attachment to the world.
“So it was then; so it is now.”
Just as you say, Bhaggava:
formerly you were a potter,
Ghaṭīkāra, in Vekaḷiṅga.
He was a supporter of his mother and father,
a lay follower of Kassapa,
and abstained from sexual intercourse.
"A celibate, free from sensual desire;
he was my fellow villager,
he was my friend in the past."
“Thus was this meeting of our ancient companions;
of us both who have developed ourselves.”
“...bearers of their final bodies.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.25 (SN 2.25, SN 106, PTS [1st ed. SN i 61, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 141) 3.
Nānātitthiyavagga (The Chapter on Various Sectarians)
The Jantu Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
on one occasion a number of bhikkhus were dwelling among the Kosalans in a forest hut on the slopes of the Himalayas.
They were arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, loose in speech, muddled in mindfulness, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds, and with unrestrained senses.
Then, on the fifteenth day of the uposatha, the deity Jantu approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he addressed those bhikkhus in verses:
“In former times they lived happily...”
The monks are disciples of Gotama;
they seek alms without desire,
and they dwell in lodgings without desire.
Having understood impermanence in the world,
they brought an end to suffering;
having made themselves difficult to nourish, [they attained liberation].
Like village headmen in a village,
they lie down after eating again and again,
infatuated with the houses of others.
Having joined my palms in reverence to the Saṅgha,
I speak here of certain ones:
they are cast aside and without a protector.
Just as the departed spirits,
so too are they. It was with reference to those who dwell in negligence that I spoke this.
"To those who dwell heedfully, I pay homage.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 2.26 (SN 2.26, SN 107, PTS [1st ed. SN i 61; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 142)
3. The Chapter on Various Sectarians.
The Discourse to Rohitassa.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Standing to one side, the young deva Rohitassa said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, where there is no birth, no aging, no death, no passing away, and no reappearing—is it possible, venerable sir, by traveling, to know, see, or reach the end of the world?
“Friend, as to where there is no birth, no aging, no death, no passing away, and no reappearing—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.”
“It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How well this has been stated by the Blessed One:
‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn—I say that the end of the world cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling.’”
“Formerly, venerable sir, I was a seer named Rohitassa, a son of the Bhojas, possessed of supernormal power and able to travel through the air.
My speed, venerable sir, was such that it was as if a skilled archer—
well-trained, practiced, and experienced, using a light arrow— were to shoot it effortlessly across [a distance].”
"I would have passed beyond the shadow of a palm tree.
Venerable sir, my stride was such that it was as if from the eastern ocean to the western ocean.
Venerable sir, such a desire arose in me:"
‘I shall reach the end of the world by traveling.
Yet, Bhante, although I possessed such speed and such a stride, apart from eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting;
apart from the business of defecation and urination; and apart from dispelling drowsiness and fatigue—
"Having a lifespan of a hundred years, living for a hundred years, and having traveled for a hundred years, he passed away in the interval without even reaching the end of the world.
It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One:"
“‘Friend, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and does not reappear—to that end of the world, I say, one cannot go in order to know it, to see it, or to reach it.
‘But, friend, I do not say that the making of an end to suffering occurs without reaching the end of the world.

Rather, friend, it is in this very fathom-long carcass, endowed with perception and mind, that I describe the world, the origin of the world, the cessation of the world, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.’”
The end of the world can never be reached by traveling; yet,
without reaching the end of the world, [suffering cannot be overcome].
There is liberation from suffering.
Therefore, indeed, the wise one who knows the world,
having reached the end of the world and lived the holy life, [should train].
“Having known the end of the world,
the one who has attained peace does not long for this world or the next.”
3. Nānātitthiyavagga Nandasutta Standing to one side,
the young deva Nanda recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“The nights pass away, their dark moments fleeting;
the qualities of youth are abandoned one after another.
Perceiving this danger in death, [one should strive].”
“One should perform deeds that bring about happiness.
“Time passes, the nights hasten by;
the qualities of youth are gradually abandoned.”
Perceiving this danger in death,
one who seeks peace should abandon the bait of the world.
3. The Chapter on Various Sectarians.
The Nandivisāla Sutta.
Standing to one side, the young deva Nandivisāla addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“Having four wheels and nine gates,
filled and joined with greed,
O Great Hero, it is born in the mire.”
“How will there be a journey?
[The answer: “Having cut through the thong and the strap, as well as evil desire and greed;”
“Having uprooted craving together with its root, in this way one’s livelihood will be sustained.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.29 (SN 2.29, SN 110, PTS [1st ed. SN i 63, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 146)
3. The Chapter on Various Sectarians.
The Discourse to Susīma.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, do you also approve of Sāriputta?
“Bhante, who indeed—unless they were foolish, hateful, deluded, or possessed of a perverted mind—would not approve of the Venerable Sāriputta?”
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is wise.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta possesses great wisdom.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta possesses vast wisdom.
Venerable Sāriputta, Bhante, possesses a smile-like wisdom;
Venerable Sāriputta, Bhante, possesses fleet-footed wisdom;
Venerable Sāriputta, Bhante, possesses sharp wisdom.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, possesses penetrative wisdom.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, has few desires.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, is contented.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is secluded.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is unattached.
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is resolute in energy.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, is patient with what is said.
Venerable Sāriputta, bhante, is a reprover.
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is one who censures evil.
For what wise person, venerable sir—who is not foolish, not hateful, not deluded, and whose mind is not perverted—would he not find approval?
“It is so, Ānanda; it is so, Ānanda.”
For who indeed, Ānanda—unless they were foolish, hateful, deluded, or possessed of a perverted mind—would not approve of Sāriputta?
Wise, Ānanda, is Sāriputta;
possessed of great wisdom, Ānanda, is Sāriputta.
Ānanda, Sāriputta has broad wisdom.
Ānanda, Sāriputta has joyful wisdom.
Ānanda, Sāriputta has swift wisdom.
Sāriputta, Ānanda, possesses sharp wisdom.
Sāriputta, Ānanda, possesses penetrative wisdom.
Sāriputta, Ānanda, has few desires.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is contented.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is secluded.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is unentangled.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is one who has aroused energy.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is one who encourages others.
Ānanda, Sāriputta is one who is patient with what is said to him.
“Ānanda, Sāriputta is one who reproves;
Ānanda, Sāriputta is one who censures evil.
For what wise person, Ānanda—unless they were foolish, hateful, deluded, or deranged—would not find Sāriputta to their liking?”
Then, while the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the young deva Susīma, surrounded by a great assembly of young devas, approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the young deva Susīma addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
For who, venerable sir, that is not foolish, not corrupt, not deluded, and not of perverted mind—whom would the Venerable Sāriputta not please?
Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is wise.”
Venerable sir, he is one of great wisdom, of broad wisdom, of smiling wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom, and of penetrative wisdom;
venerable sir, he is of few wishes, contented, secluded, unattached, energetic, a speaker, and patient with being spoken to.
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is one who reproves for evil; venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is one who censures evil.
For what wise person, venerable sir—who is not wicked, not deluded, and whose mind is not perverted—would the Venerable Sāriputta not please?
Indeed, venerable sir, whatever assembly of sons of gods I approach, it is this very sound that I most frequently hear:"
‘The Venerable Sāriputta is wise;
the Venerable One has great wisdom, broad wisdom, radiant wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, penetrative wisdom;
the Venerable One is of few desires, contented, and secluded.’
“The Venerable One is unattached; the Venerable One has aroused energy; the Venerable One is a speaker; the Venerable One is patient with speech;
the Venerable One is an admonisher; the Venerable Sāriputta is one who censures evil.
“Venerable sir, what wise person indeed—unless they were foolish, hateful, deluded, or possessed of a perverted mind—would not find the Venerable Sāriputta pleasing?”

Then, as the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the assembly of Susīma’s fellow devas were uplifted, gladdened, and filled with joy and happiness; they manifested various kinds of radiant splendor.
Just as a beautiful, well-born beryl gem, eight-faceted and well-polished, placed upon a yellow cloth, gleams, blazes, and radiates light; so too did they manifest their splendor.

In this very way, as the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the assembly of the young god Susīma became elated, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness, manifesting various kinds of radiant complexions.
Just as a piece of gold from the Jambu River, skillfully refined in the furnace by a clever smith’s apprentice and placed upon a yellow cloth, shines, glows, and radiates; so too did they appear.

In this very way, as the assembly of the young deva Susīma heard the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta being spoken, they were uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness, manifesting various splendors of complexion.
It was just as when, in the autumn season, the sky is clear and free from clouds, at the time of dawn, the medicinal star (the moon) shines, glows, and radiates light.

In the same way, as the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the assembly of the young deva Susīma—elated, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness—displayed various radiant complexions.

Just as in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free from clouds, the sun, rising into the heavens, dispels all the darkness in the atmosphere and shines, glows, and radiates with brilliance; so too did that assembly appear.

In this very way, as the praise of the Venerable Sāriputta was being spoken, the assembly of the divine son Susīma became uplifted, joyful, and filled with rapture and gladness, manifesting various kinds of radiant complexions.
Then the divine son Susīma, concerning the Venerable Sāriputta, recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“He is renowned as wise, ... [text continues] ...”
Sāriputta is free from anger;
he has few desires, is gentle, self-controlled,
and is an ascetic adorned with the Teacher’s praise.
Then the Blessed One, concerning the venerable Sāriputta, replied to the young deity Susīma with a verse:
“Sāriputta is known as wise, free from anger;”
“Having few desires, gentle, tamed, well-tamed, he awaits his time.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 2.30 (SN 2.30, SN 111, PTS [1st ed. SN i 65; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 151)
3. The Chapter on Various Non-Buddhist Sectarians: The Discourse on the Disciples of Various Non-Buddhist Sectarians.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Then several young devas who were disciples of various other sects— Asama, Sahali, Nīka, Ākoṭaka, Vegabbhari, and Māṇavagāmiya— at the end of the night,
having surpassed the radiance [of others] with their own surpassing beauty, approached the entire extent of the Bamboo Grove.
Having illuminated the Bamboo Grove, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the deva Asama recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One concerning Pūraṇa Kassapa:
“Here, when [beings] have been cut down and slain...”
Kassapa has known this;
he perceives neither evil nor any merit for himself.
“He indeed has declared his trust;
the Teacher deserves honor.
Then the deva-son Sahali, concerning Makkhali Gosāla, spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“With self well-restrained through the loathing of asceticism,
having abandoned speech and quarreling with people;
free from the faults of deceit and crookedness, a speaker of truth— ”
“Surely he would not do such an evil deed.
Then the young deva Nīka, concerning the Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“A monk who is loathsome [of evil] and prudent...”
Well-restrained by the fourfold restraint,
explaining what has been seen and heard—
one would surely not be a doer of evil.
Then the deva-son Ākoṭaka, concerning various non-Buddhist teachers, recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Pakudhaka Kātiyāna, Nigaṇṭha,
and these Makkhali and Pūraṇa;”
“The teachers of the assembly have attained the state of recluseship;
surely they are not far from being true men.
Then the devaputta Vegabbhari replied to the devaputta Ākoṭaka with a verse:
“Though he associates with them, the wretched jackal is never equal to the lion;
naked, a speaker of falsehood, and a teacher of the multitude.”
“The conduct of Saṅkassa is not like that of the virtuous.
Then Māra the Evil One, having possessed the devaputta Begabbhari, recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Devoted to self-mortification and loathing [of the world],”
Protecting your solitude,
[be mindful] of those who are attached to forms and who delight in the world of the gods.
“They indeed instruct them rightly for the sake of the world beyond, O mother.
Then the Blessed One, having recognized, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One with a verse:
“Whatever forms there are here or in the world beyond,
or those of radiant color in the sky—
all of them are praised by Namuci.”
“Like bait cast for the slaughter of fish.
Then the young deva Māṇavagāmiya, concerning the Blessed One, recited these verses in the presence of the Blessed One:
“The one who is vast among those of Rājagaha...”
The best of mountains is called the Himalayas; the White Mountain is the best of the Himavat range;
and the sun is the best of those that travel through the sky.
The ocean is the best of bodies of water,
as the moon is among the stars;
[so is the Tathāgata] in the world together with its devas.
“The Buddha is declared the foremost.
This concludes the third chapter, the Chapter on Various Sectarians.
Its summary verse is as follows:
Siva, Khema, and Serī,
Ghaṭī, Jantu, and Rohita;
Nanda and Nandivisāla—
"Suṣīma, these ten [questions] were asked by you to various non-Buddhist teachers.
The *Devaputtasaṃyutta* is complete.
